strengths: The manuscript gives a clear constructive derivation for single-token, single-input equivalence in a Gemma-style block: the rank-1 updates to the gate/up projections reproduce the contextualized internal activation, while the RMSNorm scale update absorbs the residual-stream difference. Under the stated nonzero-activation assumptions, this core algebra is straightforward and convincing.

The layerwise induction and Algorithm 1 make the per-token construction easy to follow. The paper also appropriately acknowledges that patches must be recomputed for each history, require a contextualized forward pass, and do not constitute efficient inference or a reusable prompt compression method.

The experiments cover two architectural families, float32 and bfloat16, several text prompts, and one multimodal example. Reporting logit differences and distributional distances, rather than only top-1 agreement, is appropriate for testing numerical equivalence.

Presentation is generally polished: diagrams, equations, and appendices are legible and logically organized in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d8465b75f606443b8c228b76cce16d39/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}. The limitations section correctly distinguishes an algebraic reparameterization from a mechanism actually executed by transformers.
The work raises no substantial immediate ethical concern, and its impact discussion is proportionate to the primarily analytical contribution.
weaknesses: There is a concrete error in the claimed RMSNorm inversion result underlying the “Stable” update. Appendix B asserts that F(mu) diverges as mu approaches min_k m_k^2 from below, but this only holds if g_k m_k is nonzero for an index attaining that minimum. For example, with m=(1,2) and g=(0,1), F remains negative at that boundary, so the asserted root on the chosen interval does not exist. This is the standard hard case of sphere-constrained quadratic optimization and requires separate treatment. Consequently, the claimed universally defined unique optimum and the theoretical justification of the principal stabilization method are incomplete.

The unified theorem derives much of its apparent generality from definitions that already assume exactly the needed parameter update exists. It is a useful organizational observation, but not by itself a strong explanatory theory of in-context learning. The construction is input- and history-specific, is computed from the full-context target activations, and can encode any desired output correction into sufficiently flexible parameters; it therefore does not show that the model internally learns or “transmutes” prompts in a mechanistic sense.

The claimed connection to learning dynamics in Appendix E is largely vacuous: for a precomputed desired update Delta, the paper defines a linear pseudo-loss -Tr(Delta^T W), whose gradient is Delta by construction, together with update-specific preconditioners. Almost any prescribed parameter displacement can be represented this way. This does not establish a meaningful connection to standard optimization, an endogenous objective, or the model's actual inference computation, so statements such as “connect directly to standard learning dynamics” are unsupported.

Architectural universality is overclaimed. The MoE lemma assumes fixed router gates and output-controllable experts, but the manuscript does not rigorously handle input-dependent routing, top-k selection discontinuities, or changes in the active expert set. More broadly, most listed architectures are covered only by schematic algebra, while end-to-end tests are limited to Gemma and Falcon.

The evaluation is too small and incompletely documented to substantiate broad empirical claims: it uses only five hand-selected textual prompts, one displayed image example, short greedy generations, and no randomized or task-level benchmark. There are no confidence intervals or clearly reported token/sample counts in the principal results. For Gemma, the baseline bfloat16 construction reaches only 87.5% token agreement, while the stable method whose derivation is incomplete is needed for 100%.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or repository is provided, and the paper omits exact checkpoint identifiers/revisions, software versions, hardware, seeds, complete decoding settings, precise prompt/chat templates, stopping criteria, and sufficient implementation detail about cache handling and extraction of token-specific layer activations. Algorithm 1 also writes Embed(C,x) as if it were a single activation without specifying sequence positions or KV-cache semantics.

Several empirical descriptions are internally unclear. “Rank distance” is defined as a Pearson rank correlation, yet plots show small values as better, suggesting that a transformed quantity such as 1-rho was actually used. The text alternates among Gemma 3 1B and 4B without fully specifying which experiments use each, and plots mostly provide distributions without accompanying numerical tables.

The paper is clearly written, but important claims repeatedly exceed what is demonstrated: exact equivalence holds only for one input/history under nonzero and controllability assumptions; experiments recompute patches using the very full-context execution being matched; and the construction offers neither context-independent weights nor computational savings. These constraints substantially reduce significance and originality relative to the framing.

Overall, the basic per-example rank-1 reparameterization is valid and potentially useful for analysis, but the incorrect optimization proof, weak interpretation of the gradient connection, overbroad architecture claims, and insufficient reproducibility are important technical and evidential weaknesses that prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Soundness: The single-block construction is transparent and largely correct under its stated nonzero-activation assumptions; the rank-1 projection updates directly reproduce the contextualized MLP inputs, while the output-scale update absorbs the residual difference.

Originality/significance: The controllability abstraction usefully organizes extensions of prior context-to-parameter equivalence results to gated MLPs, normalization variants, outer projection matrices, MoE layers, and parallel blocks. This is a modest but potentially useful conceptual generalization.

Evaluation: The paper tests Gemma and Falcon, float32 and bfloat16, text and image contexts, and includes stability and layer-depth ablations. The observed near-matching logits provide a useful implementation sanity check.

Presentation: The main construction, assumptions, and layerwise algorithm are generally easy to follow, and the paper honestly acknowledges that its updates are token-dependent, require recomputation, and should not be interpreted as the transformer literally executing this parameter-update algorithm.
Ethics: The work is primarily analytical and presents no evident material ethical concern; its impact statement is adequate for the contribution's low-risk scope.
weaknesses: Significance is substantially overstated. The patches are query/history-specific, are computed using activations from a full-context forward pass, and must be reconstructed at every generation step. Thus, the result is primarily an algebraic reparameterization of one already-computed prediction, not a reusable compilation of context, an efficient inference method, or a mechanism explaining how in-context learning arises.

The claimed connection to learning dynamics is not substantive. Appendix E defines a target-dependent linear pseudo-loss whose gradient is, by construction, the desired update, together with tailored parameter-specific preconditioners. Essentially any prescribed update can be represented this way; it does not show that ordinary training objectives, inference dynamics, or the transformer itself perform the proposed gradient steps.

There is a concrete gap in the RMSNorm inversion proof. The asserted divergence of F(mu) as mu approaches min_k m_k^2 only holds if a coordinate attaining that minimum also has g_k m_k != 0. The paper's weaker assumption that not all g_k m_k are zero does not guarantee this, so the claimed existence and uniqueness of the proposed solution are incomplete. The derivation also omits the epsilon used by practical RMSNorm implementations.

The exactness claims are blurred by implementation heuristics. When a denominator is zero, the experiments simply divide by one, which no longer implements the exact theorem. The 'stable' construction is explicitly approximate before a second potentially ill-conditioned elementwise division, yet no finite-precision error or conditioning bound supports the claim that a small residual numerator makes this division stable.

The experimental evidence is too narrow for the broad architectural and robustness claims: only five hand-selected text prompts, one image example, and two model families are evaluated. MoE and several other advertised architectures receive no empirical validation. After a token mismatch, generation is forced back onto the baseline trajectory, so the plots do not measure unconstrained rollout divergence.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript supplies no code, seeds, hardware, exact checkpoint identifiers and revisions, implementation details for cache handling or weight mutation, or clear sample counts for most box plots. Results are mainly graphical rather than numerical, making independent verification difficult.

Several empirical descriptions are imprecise: the quantity called 'rank distance' is defined as a correlation but plotted as a near-zero distance; the text alternates between sampling and argmax generation; and the evaluation does not isolate Gemma 1B versus 4B results consistently. Some appendix page headers are also visibly clipped or corrupted.

The unified theorem is close to tautological: it states that an update exists when the inner and outer functions are defined to admit exactly the required updates. The concrete lemmas add value, but they do not justify the broader claims that the framework explains how transformers 'transmute prompts into effective weights' or provides a foundation for an automated context compiler.

strengths: Soundness: The core single-block construction is simple and convincing under its stated nonzero-activation assumptions: rank-1 updates align the normalized MLP inputs, while an output-scale update absorbs the residual-stream difference. The multi-layer result then follows cleanly by induction.

Originality: Extending prior context-to-weight equivalence results to bias-free gated MLPs, RMSNorm, multi-layer networks, MoE, and parallel blocks is a useful conceptual generalization. The input/output controllability abstraction provides a convenient vocabulary for analyzing additional architectures.

Evidence: Experiments cover Gemma 3 1B/4B, Falcon-7B, float32 and bfloat16, several textual prompts, and one image-conditioned example. The precision and starting-layer ablations directly expose numerical issues rather than concealing them.
Presentation: The main argument is organized clearly, with constructive formulas, an explicit algorithm, an architectural summary table, and appendices containing proofs and numerical details.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges that the updates are query/token-specific, require recomputation, do not provide efficient inference, and do not establish that transformers literally execute this parameter-update algorithm. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Significance is limited by the token-specific nature of the equivalence. Computing a patch requires the contextual forward computation and the patch must be regenerated for every next-token history, so the result is principally an activation-matching reparameterization rather than a usable context compressor or evidence that ordinary inference performs implicit fine-tuning. Some mechanistic and explanatory claims therefore overreach the formal result.

The unified theorem is close to definitional: once f is assumed capable of exactly canceling any input change and g is assumed capable of producing any output displacement, equivalence follows immediately. The paper does not rigorously instantiate every detail of the claimed architecture coverage, such as MoE routing/top-k behavior and all normalization/residual variants in complete deployed blocks.

The exact construction requires nonzero vectors and, for the Gemma scale update, every relevant output coordinate to be nonzero. In experiments, a potential zero divisor is simply replaced by one, which no longer guarantees exact equivalence; the paper does not report how often this fallback or dangerously small denominators occur.

The RMSNorm-inversion appendix has a technical gap. Its claimed root existence on the interval below the smallest squared scale assumes that a coordinate attaining that smallest scale has nonzero g_k m_k; the stated weaker condition that not all g_k m_k vanish is insufficient. The derivation also treats a stationary solution as the unique optimum without fully handling degenerate or hard cases.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: only five text prompts and one image example are shown, with short argmax generations and no systematic task suite. Results are mostly conveyed through plots rather than exact numerical tables, and model revisions, software versions, hardware, generation lengths, seeds, and runtime/memory costs are insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is below the standard expected for an empirical component: no code or artifact is identified, and Algorithm 1 leaves implementation-critical details of ComputeSingleBlockUpdate implicit. These omissions make the reported numerical-stability results difficult to independently verify.

Overall, the core result appears technically useful and sufficiently novel for a weak accept, but the limited practical meaning, broad claims relative to the theorem, appendix gap, and incomplete reproducibility prevent a stronger recommendation.
